### Reviewer 2

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript „Forest temporal stability declines over stand age at multiple spatial scales“ by Shan et al. presents an analysis on growth variation in forest inventory and analysis (FIA) data collected across the United States. The authors present an analysis partitioning stability in three components of scale (alpha, beta, gamma), and distinguishing between components of stability and asynchrony. The question is of high relevance: how does the stability (here: in terms of tree growth, which is closely correlated to carbon uptake) of forest ecosystems change with age, and which components contribute to this stability? To do this the authors build on a framework for analyzing stability that was previously presented. Contradictory to many other works, the authors find that the stability of forest ecosystems is decreasing as they develop towards old-growth conditions. This would be an interesting finding, yet I see a number of problems with the design and analysis, essentially calling into question the strong claims of “unexpected findings” made by the authors. My main concerns are as follows:
(1) The study focuses on temporal stability of growth, which is key variable also used in seminal previous works on stability. The insurance hypothesis, for instance, was developed for a similar variable (Yachi and Loreau 1999, PNAS). However, assessing temporal stability requires data with reasonable (= moderate to high) temporal resolution. FIA data, however, have an approximate temporal resolution of one observation in 10 years. So rather than temporal variability, the study more likely assesses mid-term forest development. This, very likely, contributes to the unexpected results – see #2 below. In general, I think FIA data are not well suited for assessing the temporal stability of growth, because of their low temporal resolution.
(2) One important element of the study is the analysis across scales. I generally commend the authors for an attempt at this, as I think these kinds of multiscale studies are important. However, I again have severe doubts, whether the US FIA data are indeed well suited for this kind of analysis. Essentially, the plots that make up beta diversity in the current analysis are very close together – 36.6m from the central plot. Considering the processes that create diversity/ asynchrony at the beta level – disturbances by wildfire, insects, harvesting – and their spatial footprint, at 36.6m apart these plots are highly unlikely to capture the true beta diversity of the system, and are likely highly spatially autocorrelated. And there is a second scale consideration, this one concerning the alpha level: The individual FIA-subplots are rather small, a radius of 7.32m, so they will only have a handful of trees on them in old stands. As a consequence, it is logical that in older forests variability goes up, or stability goes down at such a small scale, because if a single tree dies in older stands, this will have a strong effect on growth (while the effect of a smaller tree dying in a younger stand is going to be much less strong, as the stem density in these stands is much higher). So I assume that your unexpected finding is – to a large degree – also an artifact of the rather small scale of analysis, relative to the size of old trees.
(3) One aspect that the authors do not talk about is how “stand age” was determined, and how certain they are in this variable. It is notoriously difficult to determine tree age, and determining stand age is even more difficult. Was a single (dominant?) tree used to determine stand age? Was age averaged across trees? Were also small trees cored or only the biggest/ most dominant trees per site? Was this averaged across species per plot? These things are relevant because age is a central variable of the current analysis, but is difficult to determine particularly in highly complex stands (i.e., late stages of stand development) that have a component of older and younger trees. Without knowing more how age was determined and how the high structural complexity of older stands was considered here it is difficult to interpret the findings presented here.
(4) The authors analyze FIA data across the US along a gradient of stand development. They do, however, not control for the fact of the particular land-use history of the US that affects the dataset they analyze. Particularly, the share of old and complex forests is higher in the Western US (which was colonized by Western people only in the 19th century), while in the Eastern US many forests are on a trajectory of recovery from past land use (as a result of the much longer western land use history in the east). Now, without controlling for this, comparing US FIA plots across stand development means comparing east (mostly young and middle-aged) to west (often old, with some young forests from fires). As the species diversity is much higher in the east, this could be another explanation for the “unexpected” pattern found by the authors.
(5) The concept that the authors used (presented previously) is interesting. I was not intimately familiar with it, and I’m afraid based on reading the authors description, I am not able to understand it completely. I perused some of the original literature, but still, I think the description (and also the equations!) need to be more clear so that the reader can understand what is going on. If we accept the concept and its indicators as is, the analyses are rather basic, mainly correlating one indicator value with another. The SEM is an exception from that, but here it is not well explained how the structure of the SEM was generated, whether other structures were tested, etc.
(6) Lastly, the wording is confusing in parts of the text, and some terms are rather uncommon (what are “conservative trees”, for instance)? Another example is in l154-155 – a lot of big words here, but what does this sentence really mean?

### Reviewer 4

Contents of the paper
The manuscript explores how the stability of net primary productivity (NPP) changes as forest become older in the Eastern portion of the United States. The authors used the US National Forest Inventory (NFI) for this purpose, using plots with repeated measurements to estimate their NPP values for the period comprised between 1995 and 2022. They convincingly show that NPP stability decreases with stand age. The authors then tested the hypothesis that stability decline can be attributed to decreasing species- and functional-diversity, and they did so at multiple spatial scales (local and metacommunity levels). The study concludes that decreasing diversity is the main driver behind decreasing stability as forests get older.
Positive remarks
I really liked the conceptual framing of this paper. The hypothesis is convincing and challenges the traditional view that forests get more stable as they become older. The argumentation behind their hypothesis is almost flawless in my opinion. The analyses seem well executed, and appropriate to answer their research questions. The narrative of the manuscript is also clear and engaging. The topic of this paper is absolutely relevant, and I think it constitutes frontier science when it comes to forest dynamics.
Points of improvement
Yet, the manuscript sacrifices scientific precision to make an engaging story. Specially when it comes to ecosystem stability, which has been a problematic concept since long ago (together with its resilience “relative”), definitions matter a lot. I don’t really disagree with their definition of stability (or what I assume they mean by this concept), but I think it’s important to clearly state what do they mean by it, since is a complex and abstract concept. Also, a number of operative definitions are missing throughout the paper: their response variable (stability of what?), their study area (which can only be really inferred from the map presented in the supplementary material), their stability metrics, the US NFI sampling design (which I had to search in internet), what do they mean by alfa, beta and gamma scales within the US NFI design, etc. Also, the study isn’t reproductible with the code provided: only the graphs and the regressions can be reproduced from it. But the difficult part is missing in the code, which is estimating the stability metrics and the functional diversity metrics. Since some parts of the methods are underexplained, I was relying on seeing this in the code, but unfortunately I still have questions about how some procedure were executed. I also missed the limitations of your study, which are many, as in any other scientific study.
General assessment of the paper
All in all, my conclusion is that this is a good paper and that it’s absolutely worth publication, here in Nature Communications or elsewhere. Is addresses a very relevant, novel and challenging question, has a great argumentation and narrative, and the analyses seem appropriate and well executed. Yet, I believe it also requires a thorough revision to ensure that all operative definitions are included, ideally on the main text. Also, the code to replicate the study should be provided in full, implying that anyone can reuse the code to extract stability measures from the US NFI data. Below, I’m including some specific remarks (major and minor) that the authors can use to improve their study, which I hope they find useful.
Congratulations on your study, and best of lucks with the revision!
Best regards,
Dr. Rodrigo Muñoz
Major remarks
1. The abstract is too technical. Try to simplify it, so anyone with a general ecological background can understand it. Also, replace the term “ecosystem stability” for “productivity stability” (or even better: NPP stability).
2. Line 153: Here you state that diversity loss produces a decrease in alfa stability, without nuances. However, what I see in your graphs is that stability decreases sharply and clearly, both for alfa and gamma metrics. Yet, functional diversity only decreases slightly, and the data look rather as a dot cloud. I know that the “FD ~ stand age” regression is significant, but that doesn’t imply that the effect is large (and here’s where you need to use common sense, not statistical metrics). I concur with you that that the decrease in Shannon and functional diversity has a role in the observed low stability of old-forests, but I disagree that this is THE cause. I think you need to expand the discussion in this sense, and think of alternative mechanisms that can affect stability, beyond biodiversity.
3. Alfa, beta and gamma spatial scales need to be defined in the body of the paper. These concepts are defined in the methods, but in the Nature Communications format, the methods are a sort of appendix. Therefore, it’s essential that these core concepts get defined in the introduction or the results.
4. Stability and their response variable, productivity, need also to be defined in the introduction. I think that the study is about above-ground primary productivity, but even after reviewing the whole study, I’m not completely sure.
5. Lines 208: As mentioned above, the study is impossible to reproduce from the code provided. It should be possible for whoever to get FIA’s data, and using your code, get to the final graphs. I know this is cumbersome, but I believe it’s a requirement for publishing in NatComm.
Minor remarks
6. Lines 67-69: Have you ever came across the paper of multiple successional pathways from John Vandermeer and colleagues? A bit old, but it reminded me a lot about your study while reading your manuscript: Vandermeer et al. 2004. Multiple basins of attraction in a tropical forest: Evidence for nonequilibrium community structure. Ecology.
7. Lines 83-86: Is this statement true? I think that, in canopy gap dynamics, the trees that get recruited when a gap is formed are rather acquisitive, especially when the gap size is large. I would say that this would increase beta and gamma diversity. Not saying is objectively true, but this is what I’d infer from my field experience.
8. Also define what do you mean by species stability and asynchrony. It can be inferred from the formulas (or so I think), but it’d be good if you provide an explanation in simple words. This can go in the methods.
9. Lines 176-178: Also dispersal limitations and environmental filtering can play a role in stand divergence.
10. Lines 186-188: Your study also uses unimodal models (i.e., regressions fitting a straight line).
11. Lines 211-216: Can you please include the sampling design diagram from the FIA’s sampling? You may include it in the Supplementary Material. I think this is important to understand what do you mean by alfa, beta and gamma “scales”.
12. Lines 219-228: Why only the plots from the Eastern portion of the US got included? Why these conditions weren’t met for the Western side? Mention this in the methods, please.
13. Lines 237-239: Please, briefly mention the properties of the indicators of alfa stability, spatial asynchrony and gamma stability in your methods. What does it mean if the metric = 1, or 0, or 5? How do I interpret the Y axis of Figures 2 and 4?
14. Lines 249: Detrend for what? I didn’t follow why the detrending was necessary in the first place.
15. Lines 277-282: What was this information used for? It isn’t completely clear from your text.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:

  2. Your original Round 1 review

## Paper

## Abstract

There is compelling experimental evidence and theoretical predictions that temporal stability of productivity, i.e., the summation of aboveground biomass growth of surviving and recruitment trees, increases with succession. However, the temporal change in productivity stability in natural forests, which may undergo functional diversity loss during canopy transition, remains unclear. Here, we use the forest inventory dataset across the eastern United States to explore how the temporal stability of forest productivity at multi-spatial scales changes with stand age during canopy transition. We find that productivity stability decreases with stand age at the local and metacommunity scales. Specifically, consistent declines in local diversity result in less asynchronous productivity dynamics among species over succession, consequently weakening local stability. Meanwhile, increasing mortality and the transition from conservative to acquisitive species with succession weaken species and local stability. Successional increases in species composition dissimilarity among local communities cause more asynchronous productivity dynamics among local communities. However, the decline in local stability surpasses the rise in asynchronous productivity dynamics among local communities, resulting in lower metacommunity stability in old forests. Our results suggest lower productivity stability in old-growth forests and highlight the urgency of protecting diversity at multiple spatial scales to maintain productivity stability.

---

## Introduction

Temporal stability of forest aboveground productivity (i.e., the ratio of mean productivity, which is the summation of aboveground biomass growth of surviving trees and in-growth by new recruitment trees, to its variation in time) is a widely accepted measure of forests’ ability to maintain productivity over time1,2. Traditional succession studies have focused on the community states, such as biomass and cover, with recent field experiments showing that their temporal stability increases with succession at multiple spatial scales3,4. However, how the temporal stability of productivity changes during late-successional stages in natural forests remains unclear at multiple spatial scales. Elucidating these dynamics will help managers ensure the stable provisioning of ecosystem services and efficient restoration practices under future conditions5–7.

Recently, a multiscale stability framework has shown that temporal stability at the larger scale (i.e., metacommunity stability) can be decomposed into temporal stability at the smaller scale (i.e., local stability) and spatial asynchrony, i.e., asynchronous productivity dynamics among local communities under heterogenous spatial environments8–10. Similarly, local stability can be decomposed into species stability and species asynchrony, i.e., temporal stability of productivity at the population level and asynchronous population dynamics in local communities. The multiscale stability framework can capture the scale dependence of ecosystem temporal stability over succession, i.e., higher stability at larger scales because deterministic processes (e.g., environmental filtering) dominate community assembly at the metacommunity scale whereas stochastic processes (e.g., random dispersal) dominate at the local scale3,11–13. However, change in temporal stability over stand age at multiple spatial scales has received little attention, particularly in late successional stages dominated by conservative species, due to the lack of long-term and nested permanent plot measurements of forest dynamics.

Increasing local species diversity and species composition dissimilarity among local communities with stand age contributes to the successional increase in metacommunity stability during early field succession experiments3,4. On the one hand, increasing canopy complexity with succession strengthens competition for light resources14,15, which promotes the coexistence of conservative species with high shade tolerance and acquisitive species with an efficient ability to utilize canopy light resources, resulting in higher local diversity16–19. Local stability tends to increase with local diversity because differentiated species functional strategies enable local communities to exhibit higher species asynchrony, i.e., the productivity gain of suitable species compensates for the productivity loss of unsuitable species (compensatory effects)1,18,20,21. On the other hand, as stands develop, stochastic processes (e.g., dispersal limitation and colonization) prompt divergent trajectories over succession among local communities22–25. Meanwhile, initial habitat heterogeneity among local communities could facilitate or inhibit the colonization of different species, resulting in higher species composition dissimilarity among local communities24,26. Dissimilarity among local communities stabilizes forest productivity against spatial environmental heterogeneity from the neighborhood scale (tens of meters) to the landscape scale (tens of kilometers), resulting in higher spatial asynchrony12,27,28. However, increasing local diversity and dissimilarity among local communities during forest succession is not always expected, especially not until late successional stages, which leads to uncertainty about the temporal stability of old forests. Decreasing local diversity and increasing dissimilarity among local communities make predicting changes in metacommunity stability during later forest succession difficult. As stands enter the canopy transition stage, overstory acquisitive species approach their lifespan and release canopy space after mortality, while understory conservative species with asymmetric competitive advantages occupy the forest canopy17,29,30. Although acquisitive species may experience increased recruitment in the understory due to their abundant seeds, their shade intolerance makes it difficult for them to occupy the canopy under the asymmetric advantage of conservative species when stand-replacing disturbances are infrequent17,31,32. This successional trajectory results in the transition from the coexistence of conservative species and acquisitive species to the dominance of conservative species, resulting in lower local diversity32–36. This diversity loss will lead to lower species asynchrony and temporal stability in local communities1,20. Meanwhile, stochastic mortality of overstory acquisitive species will allow conservative species to dominate the newly opened gap when stand-replacing disturbances are infrequent, resulting in higher species composition dissimilarity among local communities which leads to spatial asynchrony12,29,37. Previous studies have shown that increasing local stability or spatial asynchrony can both independently cause successional increases in temporal stability3,4. However, whether reduced local stability or increased spatial asynchrony contributes more to metacommunity stability is unclear.

In this work, we used the national forest survey dataset from the eastern United States to explore how stand age changes temporal stability in natural forests at multiple spatial scales (Supplementary Fig. 1). This dataset is well-suited for studying multiscale stability because each plot in the FIA program contains four circular subplots: one in the center and the other three arranged in a triangular pattern around it (Supplementary Fig. 2). We considered each subplot as a local community and each plot, comprising four subplots, as a metacommunity. Given that functional strategies can effectively capture plant responses to climate change, we used functional diversity to explore how changing diversity alters temporal stability with stand age3,38. Specifically, we examined 1) whether older forests exhibit higher temporal stability at the metacommunity and local scales (Fig. 1); and 2) whether this pattern is attributed to changes in local functional diversity and functional dissimilarity among local communities over stand age. We show decreasing diversity with forest age reduces temporal stability at multiple spatial scales, suggesting the urgency of protecting old-growth forests to ensure forest ecosystem services provisioning under climate change threats.

---

## Results

Stand age weakens temporal stability at multiple scales
We found that temporal stability of productivity at both the metacommunity scale and the local community scale decreased with stand age, but spatial asynchrony did not show a significant relationship with stand age (Fig. 2, estimate [±SE] = −0.370 [0.020], t = −15.538, P < 0.001 for local stability, estimate [±SE] = −0.582 [0.037], t = −15.538, P < 0.001 for metacommunity stability and estimate [±SE] = 0.004 [0.007], t = 0.508, P = 0.612 for spatial asynchrony). After decomposing local stability into species stability and species asynchrony, our results showed that both species stability and species asynchrony decreased with stand age (Fig. 1, estimate [±SE] = −0.258 [0.015], t = −17.655, P < 0.001 for species stability and estimate [±SE] = −0.022 [0.004], t = −5.822, P < 0.001 for species asynchrony). Besides spatial asynchrony, stand age was the major driver for stability at multiple scales (Supplementary Fig. 3A and Supplementary Table 1). Similar results were found in our sensitivity analysis which considered detrended stability (Supplementary Fig. 4), different ecoregions (Supplementary Fig. 5), other confounding variables (Supplementary Fig. 6A and Supplementary Fig. 7; observational frequency, survey interval, initial survey year, and final survey year), stand structure (Supplementary Fig. 8), and biomass loss due to mortality (Supplementary Fig. 8). Decreasing mean productivity and increasing standard deviation of productivity with stand age jointly contributed to successional declines in temporal stability (Supplementary Fig. 9 and Supplementary Fig. 10).

Stand age reduce diversity at multiple scales
Functional diversity at both the metacommunity scale and the local community scale decreased with stand age, but functional dissimilarity among local communities increased with stand age (Fig. 3, estimate [±SE] = −0.025 [0.007], t = −3.423, P < 0.001 for local functional diversity, estimate [±SE] = 0.039 [0.015], t = 2.613, P = 0.009 for functional dissimilarity among local communities, and estimate [±SE] = −0.020 [0.009], t = −2.210, P = 0.027 for metacommunity functional diversity). After considering confounding factors (observational frequency, survey interval, initial survey year, and final survey year), the trends of functional diversity with stand age at multiple spatial scales remained unchanged (Supplementary Figs. 3B, Supplementary Fig. 6B, and Supplementary Table S2). Similar results were found using the Shannon diversity index, but there was a non-significant relationship between metacommunity diversity and stand age (Fig. 3, estimate [±SE] = −0.018 [0.005], t = −3.364, P < 0.001 for local Shannon diversity, estimate [±SE] = 0.063 [0.002], t = 3.656, P < 0.001 for composition dissimilarity among local communities, and estimate [±SE] = −0.008 [0.008], t = −1.042, P = 0.297 for metacommunity Shannon diversity).

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This paper investigates how the temporal stability of forest productivity at multiple spatial scales changes with stand age and how this change is related to diversity during succession. Using a space-for-time substitution method, the authors found that the temporal stability of forest productivity decreases with stand age at both local and metacommunity scales. The findings of this study, such as older forests being less stable and the dominance of conservative species reducing species stability, differ from classic ecological theories. If accurate, these results would challenge established succession theories and our understanding of forest development in the United States. However, I recommend that the authors provide more detailed evidence supporting the reliability of their data analysis, to ensure the robustness and validity of their results and conclusions.
<General concerns>
Space-for-time substitutions, while useful, must be carefully employed. This approach has often been misused, leading to inaccurate conclusions about ecological patterns and processes (Walker et al. 2010; Damgaard 2019). Unfortunately, this paper appears to fall into this category, as it examines plots across the United States with varying ecoregions, climates, vegetation types, and soil conditions. It is challenging to believe that all these plots with different stand ages are comparable, and would follow the same successional trajectory. There are many confounding factors beyond stand age that could influence changes in diversity and stability. These factors should be considered and controlled during the analysis. For example, the authors could compare the temporal stability of plots with the same vegetation form, ecoregion, and soil type to ensure more accurate comparison. Additionally, it would be beneficial to assess whether climate and soil variables play more significant roles in driving stability changes than stand ages. The authors should perform more sensitivity analyses to validate and explain why their space-for-time substitution is valid. Without careful consideration of these factors, it is difficult to have confidence in the study’s conclusions.
The conceptual figure (Fig. 1) aligns better with the common understanding of forest succession, where community stability increases from young to mature forests and may decrease in old forests due to natural tree mortality. It is harder to believe that community stability consistently and linearly decreases over succession than to consider that the space-for-time substitution might be invalid. Given that many plots have a stand age of less than 50 years and are still in the early stages of succession, it is crucial to clarify the model selection process. Did you compare the performance of nonlinear versus linear fitting models? This comparison would help determine the most appropriate model for analyzing the relationship between stand age and stability.
Further, the detailed methodology needs better clarification. For example, stand age is a key variable in the analysis, but its definition and measurement are unclear. Was it calculated as the mean stand age of all observed years for each plot, or based on the stand age at the first or last survey? For the 2925 selected plots, how many observations were used to calculate the stability of each community, and what was the time span of these observations? How did the authors control for differences in the year of initial and last surveys, the time span, and the number of observations during the analysis? These factors could significantly influence the stability calculation and should be clearly explained to ensure robust results.
Additionally, how were α and γ diversity calculated? Were they based on the diversity of the initial year, the total, or the average of all observation years? How were the shifts in diversity during the surveys were considered?
The authors propose that the observed decrease in diversity and stability is due to a shift from co-dominance of acquisitive and conservative species to dominance by conservative species as succession progresses. This result is surprising, as it is difficult to believe that conservative trees are less stable than acquisitive trees or a mix of both. With existing trait data and methods (e.g., Díaz et al. 2016), it is crucial to directly quantify the conservative versus acquisitive strategies of each species and plot. Visualizing species composition shifts towards conservative species with increasing stand age, comparing the species stability of conservative versus acquisitive trees, and directly quantifying the effect of resource-use strategies on species and community stabilities are important steps. Additionally, the authors should provide more convincing results and explanations on why conservative trees are less stable, as this challenges the common understanding of the 'fast–slow' plant economics spectrum.
Overall, the research has the potential to make a significant impact, but the authors need to strengthen their methodological framework and provide more convincing evidence that their findings are not merely artifacts of methodological choices.
<Specific comments>

Line 19: Given that many plots have a stand age of less than 50 years, can they be accurately classified as late successional stages?
Line 22: Did functional alpha diversity increase and then decrease with stand age, or did it consistently decrease throughout succession?
Line 101: Do you mean “spatial asynchrony did not show a significant relationship with stand age”?
Line 102: It should be “P = 0.621 for spatial asynchrony”
Lines 180-195: The authors suggest that changes in environmental heterogeneity with succession might be an important factor driving spatial asynchrony. The paper already considers environmental data such as mean annual temperature and climate moisture. Calculating the variation of these environmental factors with succession would be helpful to support these arguments.

### Reviewer 2

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript „Forest temporal stability declines over stand age at multiple spatial scales“ by Shan et al. presents an analysis on growth variation in forest inventory and analysis (FIA) data collected across the United States. The authors present an analysis partitioning stability in three components of scale (alpha, beta, gamma), and distinguishing between components of stability and asynchrony. The question is of high relevance: how does the stability (here: in terms of tree growth, which is closely correlated to carbon uptake) of forest ecosystems change with age, and which components contribute to this stability? To do this the authors build on a framework for analyzing stability that was previously presented. Contradictory to many other works, the authors find that the stability of forest ecosystems is decreasing as they develop towards old-growth conditions. This would be an interesting finding, yet I see a number of problems with the design and analysis, essentially calling into question the strong claims of “unexpected findings” made by the authors. My main concerns are as follows:
(1) The study focuses on temporal stability of growth, which is key variable also used in seminal previous works on stability. The insurance hypothesis, for instance, was developed for a similar variable (Yachi and Loreau 1999, PNAS). However, assessing temporal stability requires data with reasonable (= moderate to high) temporal resolution. FIA data, however, have an approximate temporal resolution of one observation in 10 years. So rather than temporal variability, the study more likely assesses mid-term forest development. This, very likely, contributes to the unexpected results – see #2 below. In general, I think FIA data are not well suited for assessing the temporal stability of growth, because of their low temporal resolution.
(2) One important element of the study is the analysis across scales. I generally commend the authors for an attempt at this, as I think these kinds of multiscale studies are important. However, I again have severe doubts, whether the US FIA data are indeed well suited for this kind of analysis. Essentially, the plots that make up beta diversity in the current analysis are very close together – 36.6m from the central plot. Considering the processes that create diversity/ asynchrony at the beta level – disturbances by wildfire, insects, harvesting – and their spatial footprint, at 36.6m apart these plots are highly unlikely to capture the true beta diversity of the system, and are likely highly spatially autocorrelated. And there is a second scale consideration, this one concerning the alpha level: The individual FIA-subplots are rather small, a radius of 7.32m, so they will only have a handful of trees on them in old stands. As a consequence, it is logical that in older forests variability goes up, or stability goes down at such a small scale, because if a single tree dies in older stands, this will have a strong effect on growth (while the effect of a smaller tree dying in a younger stand is going to be much less strong, as the stem density in these stands is much higher). So I assume that your unexpected finding is – to a large degree – also an artifact of the rather small scale of analysis, relative to the size of old trees.
(3) One aspect that the authors do not talk about is how “stand age” was determined, and how certain they are in this variable. It is notoriously difficult to determine tree age, and determining stand age is even more difficult. Was a single (dominant?) tree used to determine stand age? Was age averaged across trees? Were also small trees cored or only the biggest/ most dominant trees per site? Was this averaged across species per plot? These things are relevant because age is a central variable of the current analysis, but is difficult to determine particularly in highly complex stands (i.e., late stages of stand development) that have a component of older and younger trees. Without knowing more how age was determined and how the high structural complexity of older stands was considered here it is difficult to interpret the findings presented here.
(4) The authors analyze FIA data across the US along a gradient of stand development. They do, however, not control for the fact of the particular land-use history of the US that affects the dataset they analyze. Particularly, the share of old and complex forests is higher in the Western US (which was colonized by Western people only in the 19th century), while in the Eastern US many forests are on a trajectory of recovery from past land use (as a result of the much longer western land use history in the east). Now, without controlling for this, comparing US FIA plots across stand development means comparing east (mostly young and middle-aged) to west (often old, with some young forests from fires). As the species diversity is much higher in the east, this could be another explanation for the “unexpected” pattern found by the authors.
(5) The concept that the authors used (presented previously) is interesting. I was not intimately familiar with it, and I’m afraid based on reading the authors description, I am not able to understand it completely. I perused some of the original literature, but still, I think the description (and also the equations!) need to be more clear so that the reader can understand what is going on. If we accept the concept and its indicators as is, the analyses are rather basic, mainly correlating one indicator value with another. The SEM is an exception from that, but here it is not well explained how the structure of the SEM was generated, whether other structures were tested, etc.
(6) Lastly, the wording is confusing in parts of the text, and some terms are rather uncommon (what are “conservative trees”, for instance)? Another example is in l154-155 – a lot of big words here, but what does this sentence really mean?

### Reviewer 4

Contents of the paper
The manuscript explores how the stability of net primary productivity (NPP) changes as forest become older in the Eastern portion of the United States. The authors used the US National Forest Inventory (NFI) for this purpose, using plots with repeated measurements to estimate their NPP values for the period comprised between 1995 and 2022. They convincingly show that NPP stability decreases with stand age. The authors then tested the hypothesis that stability decline can be attributed to decreasing species- and functional-diversity, and they did so at multiple spatial scales (local and metacommunity levels). The study concludes that decreasing diversity is the main driver behind decreasing stability as forests get older.
Positive remarks
I really liked the conceptual framing of this paper. The hypothesis is convincing and challenges the traditional view that forests get more stable as they become older. The argumentation behind their hypothesis is almost flawless in my opinion. The analyses seem well executed, and appropriate to answer their research questions. The narrative of the manuscript is also clear and engaging. The topic of this paper is absolutely relevant, and I think it constitutes frontier science when it comes to forest dynamics.
Points of improvement
Yet, the manuscript sacrifices scientific precision to make an engaging story. Specially when it comes to ecosystem stability, which has been a problematic concept since long ago (together with its resilience “relative”), definitions matter a lot. I don’t really disagree with their definition of stability (or what I assume they mean by this concept), but I think it’s important to clearly state what do they mean by it, since is a complex and abstract concept. Also, a number of operative definitions are missing throughout the paper: their response variable (stability of what?), their study area (which can only be really inferred from the map presented in the supplementary material), their stability metrics, the US NFI sampling design (which I had to search in internet), what do they mean by alfa, beta and gamma scales within the US NFI design, etc. Also, the study isn’t reproductible with the code provided: only the graphs and the regressions can be reproduced from it. But the difficult part is missing in the code, which is estimating the stability metrics and the functional diversity metrics. Since some parts of the methods are underexplained, I was relying on seeing this in the code, but unfortunately I still have questions about how some procedure were executed. I also missed the limitations of your study, which are many, as in any other scientific study.
General assessment of the paper
All in all, my conclusion is that this is a good paper and that it’s absolutely worth publication, here in Nature Communications or elsewhere. Is addresses a very relevant, novel and challenging question, has a great argumentation and narrative, and the analyses seem appropriate and well executed. Yet, I believe it also requires a thorough revision to ensure that all operative definitions are included, ideally on the main text. Also, the code to replicate the study should be provided in full, implying that anyone can reuse the code to extract stability measures from the US NFI data. Below, I’m including some specific remarks (major and minor) that the authors can use to improve their study, which I hope they find useful.
Congratulations on your study, and best of lucks with the revision!
Best regards,
Dr. Rodrigo Muñoz
Major remarks
1. The abstract is too technical. Try to simplify it, so anyone with a general ecological background can understand it. Also, replace the term “ecosystem stability” for “productivity stability” (or even better: NPP stability).
2. Line 153: Here you state that diversity loss produces a decrease in alfa stability, without nuances. However, what I see in your graphs is that stability decreases sharply and clearly, both for alfa and gamma metrics. Yet, functional diversity only decreases slightly, and the data look rather as a dot cloud. I know that the “FD ~ stand age” regression is significant, but that doesn’t imply that the effect is large (and here’s where you need to use common sense, not statistical metrics). I concur with you that that the decrease in Shannon and functional diversity has a role in the observed low stability of old-forests, but I disagree that this is THE cause. I think you need to expand the discussion in this sense, and think of alternative mechanisms that can affect stability, beyond biodiversity.
3. Alfa, beta and gamma spatial scales need to be defined in the body of the paper. These concepts are defined in the methods, but in the Nature Communications format, the methods are a sort of appendix. Therefore, it’s essential that these core concepts get defined in the introduction or the results.
4. Stability and their response variable, productivity, need also to be defined in the introduction. I think that the study is about above-ground primary productivity, but even after reviewing the whole study, I’m not completely sure.
5. Lines 208: As mentioned above, the study is impossible to reproduce from the code provided. It should be possible for whoever to get FIA’s data, and using your code, get to the final graphs. I know this is cumbersome, but I believe it’s a requirement for publishing in NatComm.
Minor remarks
6. Lines 67-69: Have you ever came across the paper of multiple successional pathways from John Vandermeer and colleagues? A bit old, but it reminded me a lot about your study while reading your manuscript: Vandermeer et al. 2004. Multiple basins of attraction in a tropical forest: Evidence for nonequilibrium community structure. Ecology.
7. Lines 83-86: Is this statement true? I think that, in canopy gap dynamics, the trees that get recruited when a gap is formed are rather acquisitive, especially when the gap size is large. I would say that this would increase beta and gamma diversity. Not saying is objectively true, but this is what I’d infer from my field experience.
8. Also define what do you mean by species stability and asynchrony. It can be inferred from the formulas (or so I think), but it’d be good if you provide an explanation in simple words. This can go in the methods.
9. Lines 176-178: Also dispersal limitations and environmental filtering can play a role in stand divergence.
10. Lines 186-188: Your study also uses unimodal models (i.e., regressions fitting a straight line).
11. Lines 211-216: Can you please include the sampling design diagram from the FIA’s sampling? You may include it in the Supplementary Material. I think this is important to understand what do you mean by alfa, beta and gamma “scales”.
12. Lines 219-228: Why only the plots from the Eastern portion of the US got included? Why these conditions weren’t met for the Western side? Mention this in the methods, please.
13. Lines 237-239: Please, briefly mention the properties of the indicators of alfa stability, spatial asynchrony and gamma stability in your methods. What does it mean if the metric = 1, or 0, or 5? How do I interpret the Y axis of Figures 2 and 4?
14. Lines 249: Detrend for what? I didn’t follow why the detrending was necessary in the first place.
15. Lines 277-282: What was this information used for? It isn’t completely clear from your text.
16. Lines 293: How did you defined the ecoregions? It’s the first, and probably the last, time that the term appeared in the manuscript.

Thirdly, as suggested, we evaluated the importance of forest age and environmental variables (climate and soil variables) in explaining model variance, and found that stand ages played more significant roles in determining multiscale stability than environmental variables (Fig. S3; lines 114-115).
Finally, in the discussion section, we also noted the potential limitation of space-for-time approach: “First, the space-for-time approach we employed is often criticized for potentially overlooking different successional trajectories across varied environments. To address this limitation, we conducted separate analyses for ecoregions with similar environmental conditions and potential communities, leading to consistent conclusions (Fig. S5). Further research extending single time series into late successional stages would be valuable for generalizing the observed patterns” (lines 225-229).

RESPONSE: Thank you for the comment. In our initial analysis, we compared the performance of nonlinear (logarithmic and quadratic transformed stand age) versus linear functions describing the temporal trend of stability at multiple spatial scales, based on Akaike information criterion (AIC; lines 380-384; Table S1). We found that all three models performed similarly (with similar AIC; Table S1) and showed a consistent decrease in stability with forest age (Fig. S6). The continuous decrease in stability with forest age may be because our plots were generally concentrated in the canopy transition stage (Fig. S19 and S20, mainly 30-100 years), where the early acquisitive trees changed to the late conservative species (Fig. S19) and species diversity decreases (Fig. 3). Considering the simplicity and interpretability, we choose to use the untransformed stand age in the main text, and presented the logarithmic and quadratic transformed results in the appendix (Fig. S22). ### Reviewer 1

I would like to thank the authors for their detailed responses and the additional analyses they provided. The manuscript has improved significantly in clarity and data analysis rigor. I appreciate the authors' efforts, particularly in incorporating sensitivity analyses to address the limitations of the space-for-time substitution method. However, I have a few additional comments for further consideration.
1. Sensitivity Analyses: The authors have made commendable efforts to conduct additional sensitivity analyses, including the integration of soil and climate variables and analyses across different ecoregions. However, these analyses come across as largely descriptive and complex. The current approach, which examines confounding variables individually, does not capture their combined effects, resulting in a total of 23 supplementary figures that may overwhelm readers. I strongly recommend that the authors adopt a unified linear mixed effects model to evaluate the impacts of stand age and all confounding variables simultaneously. This approach would facilitate a clearer comparison of their relative importance (see Figure 4 in https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-017-0132 for reference). Instead of analyzing confounding variables one by one, the authors could add survey interval, observational span, initial and final survey years, and observational frequency as fixed or random effects in the same model (Line 371). A model selection procedure could then identify the best predictors of stability and diversity and assess the relative importance of all fixed effects considered as drivers of these components. This would provide clearer evidence regarding the significance of stand age when accounting for confounding variables and highlight which other variables are important in determining stability and diversity relative to stand age.
2. Definition of Concepts. I concur with the other reviewers that the concepts utilized in the study require clearer definitions, particularly regarding the term "temporal stability." This distinction is crucial, as classic succession theory and empirical studies focus on the status of communities (e.g., temporal stability of composition, biomass, and cover), whereas this study emphasizes the change rate of the community (i.e., invariability of annual biomass growth), which may diverge from the classical definition. According to classic succession theory, late successional communities are expected to reach equilibrium, potentially leading to minimal biomass growth. In this context, the temporal stability of productivity, measured by the mean to standard deviation ratio, would also be expected to decrease in late successional communities. While I do not dispute the authors' approach, it is essential to clarify how their definition of stability differs from traditional theories. Additionally, some fundamental results and data are missing, making it challenging to evaluate consistency with classic succession theory. I recommend the authors include basic information, such as how biomass and annual productivity (along with their standard deviation) change with stand age, and whether decreased stability is driven by reduced productivity or increased standard deviation. Providing this context will enhance readers' understanding of the observed patterns. If decreased stability is primarily due to lower annual biomass growth, this study may support rather than challenge traditional succession theories.
3. Functional Trait Analysis. I appreciate the authors' attempt to use PCA based on functional traits to capture species' adaptive strategies and to conduct structural equation models (SEMs) to explore how these strategies change with stand age and influence stability. However, In the PCA of S21A, the authors suggest that "The first axis (CWMPC1) represents traits associated with broad-leaved strategies (high SLA, Nmass, Pmass, and low LDMC), while the second axis (CWMPC2) refers to traits associated with acquisitive strategies (low WD)." This interpretation may be incorrect. According to the well-accepted leaf economic spectrum, the LDMC-Nmass dimension reflects the acquisitive-conservative continuum (e.g., Diaz et al. 2016). Therefore, A more accurate interpretation is needed to enhance the study's reliability.
Minor comments:
Line 1: The authors should clarify in the title that this study focuses specifically on the temporal stability of productivity (i.e., annual biomass growth rate) rather than other components of temporal stability.
Lines 178-187: This section requires substantial revision, as PC1 (the LDMC-Nmass dimension) reflects the acquisitive-conservative continuum, not PC2 (the WD dimension).
Line 258: This claim may not hold true; even within the same ecoregion, plots can differ significantly in terms of land use, climate, physiography, lithology, soils, and potential natural communities.
Line 260: How is aboveground biomass measured in this study?
Lines 336-339: The definition provided differs from the commonly accepted understanding of the leaf economic spectrum. Why not consider the positive correlations with CWMSLA, CWMNmass, and CWMPmass, alongside the negative correlation with CWMLDMC, as indicators of acquisitive strategies, as is typically done?
Line 347: Since functional dispersion is a distance-based index of functional diversity that operates largely independently of species richness, please verify whether it allows for a multiplicative partitioning of diversity into gamma, alpha, and beta components, and clarify how this can be achieved (see Chao et al. 2019, Ecol. Monogr. 89: e01343).

A model selection procedure using the ‘dredge’ function from the R package MuMIn could then identify the best predictors. This would allow for a clear comparison of the relative importance of predictors (such as stand age, temperature, and soil properties) to determine whether stand age is a key driver of the temporal stability of productivity in US forests.
Overall, the authors have made commendable strides in addressing the study's limitations, enhancing its robustness. I remain optimistic about the manuscript, though the strong claim regarding the challenge to the traditional view of forest succession requires further substantiation. A more thorough analysis and additional details will clarify the dynamics at play in these plots and their implications for traditional succession theory.

### Reviewer 3

I have reviewed a previous version of this manuscript, and was rather critical about many of the assumptions and conclusions drawn. In their revision, the authors did a good job in addressing some of my major concerns. These were specifically (numbering following my initial comments):
(3) Stand age: The authors now clarify how stand age was determined, which is important for contextualizing the results of the paper. Also, the authors conducted an additional sensitivity analysis looking into the effect of stand structural complexity (which is often associated with age), which is great.
(4) US FIA data: The authors stated (and still state) in the abstract and in the objectives section at the end of the introduction that they are analyzing US FIA data, which led me to believe that we are talking the entirety of the US. In their response they clarify that they only focused on the Eastern US, which makes some of my comments on the original version moot. This is now clearer for me, but the revised version still talks about “US” in many places, e.g. line 17 (“forest inventory dataset across the United States”) or line 95 (“the national forest survey dataset from the United States”), which is highly misleading to the reader. Please don’t oversell, but state clearly what your study area was throughout the text!
(5) Explanation of the concept: This is now better explained and better to follow, thanks!
(6) Wording: Some of the wording choices that were confusing to me are now rectified, thank you very much! Nonetheless, parts of the text still have grammatical errors and the manuscript would overall benefit a close read of a native speaker, if available.
However, there are also elements where my initial concerns were not really addressed in the revision. This is mostly because they are fundamental concerns that are related to the data, and how the data is used in the context of the concept applied here. I will reiterate here why I think there are inherent problems with these issues.
(1) Time scale: Thank you for clarifying the – on average – five-year remeasurement interval in your data. I still maintain, that 5-10 year averages are not able to represent temporal stability of growth, particularly since you frame the analyses strongly in the context of environmental fluctuations (e.g., in lines 38, 53, 70, 101 etc.). These fluctuations that you aim to study stability against happen at a much finer temporal grain, and will not be visible at the grain of your analysis, where they will be strongly masked by other trends (such as those of succession). So I do think that framing the results in the context of stability is misleading. In your rebuttal you use the argument that somebody else has done the same (mostly one author, Qiao et al.) – well, this doesn’t make it better, to be honest. Furthermore, the sensitivity analysis you’ve added is not helpful here, as it goes up in survey interval (from 5 to ten years), while the actual question is about higher frequency data, i.e. shorter survey intervals. So fundamentally I think the framing around temporal stability and environmental fluctuations is misleading.
(2) Spatial scale: Although I do not agree I can accept the point on the different spatial levels. This negates large parts of ecological research and will confuse many readers (that think about much larger scales when they read beta or gamma diversity), but the scales are well defined in the text, so there’s that. My fundamental criticism, however, is even stronger than for #1 above: I maintain that your “unexpected” results are simply the result of the small scale of your analysis. Treating the small subplots of FIA as a single analysis entity and considering the average size of a fully grown tree, variability at the sub-plot level have to go up with age, simply because a single tree dying (or declining in growth) will have a much larger share on the plot area then in younger stand development stages. Please note that the initial design of the FIA was not to analyze subplots individually, but to jointly analyze all four plots together as a single analysis entity. So I inherently think that the design of the inventory (which was not done by the authors) is driving the results, and what we see is mainly an effect of the plot design. This, to me, is underscored by the fact that in all the sensitivity analyses that the authors have added, there is hardly any variation, across all the variables tested. Again, the fact that another author (the same one mentioned already in the other point above) did something like this before does not make it better.
To conclude I truly appreciate the authors for their efforts in the revision. I nonetheless think that there are fundamental flaws in the analysis, particularly regarding the assumptions of scale, that drive the results. I cannot help but feel that this is a classical case of the fallacy of “have pet concept, will apply to any data”, i.e., not considering the limitations of the data for the sake of implementing a certain concept.

### Reviewer 4

I am reviewing this study for the second time. I went through the rebuttal letter in response to the review provided by the four reviewers of this manuscript, and through the manuscript once again to assess the changes implemented. I believe the authors did a great job specially in their rebuttal letter, giving detailed responses to most of our comments. I am satisfied in general with their responses and I believe that most of my concerns where either addressed in the manuscript or argued against in an convincing manner.
Yet, after reading the four reviews and their answers, I have to agree with Reviewer # 3 on an important point: there are problems with the concepts of beta and gamma diversity (Rev 3, point 2). I envision the concepts of alpha, beta, and gamma diversity from a landscape perspective, which is not in line with how the authors use the concepts (please refer to the abstract on Sepkoski 1988 for a very straightforward definition of these). Actually, I think that each FIA sampling unit (i.e., the four sub-plots in a triangular arrange) is intended to capture the variability within a forest patch. However, the concept of beta diversity is intended to capture the variability across different patches within a landscape, while gamma diversity reflects the diversity in a defined landscape. In this study, we can’t really speak about beta and gamma diversities in my opinion, since the four-subplot design intends to provide a more robust estimate of properties in a single forest patch. This doesn’t imply that the study results are not valid, but rather that the concepts used in the manuscript need to be clarified and probably modified in accordance to how these concepts are defined in ecological theory.
In their response to Reviewer 3, the authors refer repeatedly to studies by Qiao et al. While it’s good that the authors anchor their operative definitions to the work of others, it’s important they go beyond just a single group of researchers. Quite possibly, they would find that most other authors assess diversity scales from a landscape perspective.
For the rest, I would only suggest the authors to carefully check the writing of the new text segments, as I found some writing mistakes, in contrast to the original version which was very well polished.
I hope this new assessment helps the authors reach a decision about the manuscript, and the authors to continue improving their manuscript. I was already very positive about this study, and I maintain this assessment in this new version.

## Paper

## Abstract

There is compelling experimental evidence and theoretical predictions that temporal stability of productivity, i.e., the summation of aboveground biomass growth of surviving and recruitment trees, increases with succession. However, the temporal change in productivity stability in natural forests, which may undergo functional diversity loss during canopy transition, remains unclear. Here, we use the forest inventory dataset across the eastern United States to explore how the temporal stability of forest productivity at multi-spatial scales changes with stand age during canopy transition. We find that productivity stability decreases with stand age at the local and metacommunity scales. Specifically, consistent declines in local diversity result in less asynchronous productivity dynamics among species over succession, consequently weakening local stability. Meanwhile, increasing mortality and the transition from conservative to acquisitive species with succession weaken species and local stability. Successional increases in species composition dissimilarity among local communities cause more asynchronous productivity dynamics among local communities. However, the decline in local stability surpasses the rise in asynchronous productivity dynamics among local communities, resulting in lower metacommunity stability in old forests. Our results suggest lower productivity stability in old-growth forests and highlight the urgency of protecting diversity at multiple spatial scales to maintain productivity stability.

---

## Introduction

Temporal stability of forest aboveground productivity (i.e., the ratio of mean productivity, which is the summation of aboveground biomass growth of surviving trees and in-growth by new recruitment trees, to its variation in time) is a widely accepted measure of forests’ ability to maintain productivity over time1,2. Traditional succession studies have focused on the community states, such as biomass and cover, with recent field experiments showing that their temporal stability increases with succession at multiple spatial scales3,4. However, how the temporal stability of productivity changes during late-successional stages in natural forests remains unclear at multiple spatial scales. Elucidating these dynamics will help managers ensure the stable provisioning of ecosystem services and efficient restoration practices under future conditions5–7.

Recently, a multiscale stability framework has shown that temporal stability at the larger scale (i.e., metacommunity stability) can be decomposed into temporal stability at the smaller scale (i.e., local stability) and spatial asynchrony, i.e., asynchronous productivity dynamics among local communities under heterogenous spatial environments8–10. Similarly, local stability can be decomposed into species stability and species asynchrony, i.e., temporal stability of productivity at the population level and asynchronous population dynamics in local communities. The multiscale stability framework can capture the scale dependence of ecosystem temporal stability over succession, i.e., higher stability at larger scales because deterministic processes (e.g., environmental filtering) dominate community assembly at the metacommunity scale whereas stochastic processes (e.g., random dispersal) dominate at the local scale3,11–13. However, change in temporal stability over stand age at multiple spatial scales has received little attention, particularly in late successional stages dominated by conservative species, due to the lack of long-term and nested permanent plot measurements of forest dynamics.

Increasing local species diversity and species composition dissimilarity among local communities with stand age contributes to the successional increase in metacommunity stability during early field succession experiments3,4. On the one hand, increasing canopy complexity with succession strengthens competition for light resources14,15, which promotes the coexistence of conservative species with high shade tolerance and acquisitive species with an efficient ability to utilize canopy light resources, resulting in higher local diversity16–19. Local stability tends to increase with local diversity because differentiated species functional strategies enable local communities to exhibit higher species asynchrony, i.e., the productivity gain of suitable species compensates for the productivity loss of unsuitable species (compensatory effects)1,18,20,21. On the other hand, as stands develop, stochastic processes (e.g., dispersal limitation and colonization) prompt divergent trajectories over succession among local communities22–25. Meanwhile, initial habitat heterogeneity among local communities could facilitate or inhibit the colonization of different species, resulting in higher species composition dissimilarity among local communities24,26. Dissimilarity among local communities stabilizes forest productivity against spatial environmental heterogeneity from the neighborhood scale (tens of meters) to the landscape scale (tens of kilometers), resulting in higher spatial asynchrony12,27,28. However, increasing local diversity and dissimilarity among local communities during forest succession is not always expected, especially not until late successional stages, which leads to uncertainty about the temporal stability of old forests. Decreasing local diversity and increasing dissimilarity among local communities make predicting changes in metacommunity stability during later forest succession difficult. As stands enter the canopy transition stage, overstory acquisitive species approach their lifespan and release canopy space after mortality, while understory conservative species with asymmetric competitive advantages occupy the forest canopy17,29,30. Although acquisitive species may experience increased recruitment in the understory due to their abundant seeds, their shade intolerance makes it difficult for them to occupy the canopy under the asymmetric advantage of conservative species when stand-replacing disturbances are infrequent17,31,32. This successional trajectory results in the transition from the coexistence of conservative species and acquisitive species to the dominance of conservative species, resulting in lower local diversity32–36. This diversity loss will lead to lower species asynchrony and temporal stability in local communities1,20. Meanwhile, stochastic mortality of overstory acquisitive species will allow conservative species to dominate the newly opened gap when stand-replacing disturbances are infrequent, resulting in higher species composition dissimilarity among local communities which leads to spatial asynchrony12,29,37. Previous studies have shown that increasing local stability or spatial asynchrony can both independently cause successional increases in temporal stability3,4. However, whether reduced local stability or increased spatial asynchrony contributes more to metacommunity stability is unclear.

In this work, we used the national forest survey dataset from the eastern United States to explore how stand age changes temporal stability in natural forests at multiple spatial scales (Supplementary Fig. 1). This dataset is well-suited for studying multiscale stability because each plot in the FIA program contains four circular subplots: one in the center and the other three arranged in a triangular pattern around it (Supplementary Fig. 2). We considered each subplot as a local community and each plot, comprising four subplots, as a metacommunity. Given that functional strategies can effectively capture plant responses to climate change, we used functional diversity to explore how changing diversity alters temporal stability with stand age3,38. Specifically, we examined 1) whether older forests exhibit higher temporal stability at the metacommunity and local scales (Fig. 1); and 2) whether this pattern is attributed to changes in local functional diversity and functional dissimilarity among local communities over stand age. We show decreasing diversity with forest age reduces temporal stability at multiple spatial scales, suggesting the urgency of protecting old-growth forests to ensure forest ecosystem services provisioning under climate change threats.

---

## Results

Stand age weakens temporal stability at multiple scales
We found that temporal stability of productivity at both the metacommunity scale and the local community scale decreased with stand age, but spatial asynchrony did not show a significant relationship with stand age (Fig. 2, estimate [±SE] = −0.370 [0.020], t = −15.538, P < 0.001 for local stability, estimate [±SE] = −0.582 [0.037], t = −15.538, P < 0.001 for metacommunity stability and estimate [±SE] = 0.004 [0.007], t = 0.508, P = 0.612 for spatial asynchrony). After decomposing local stability into species stability and species asynchrony, our results showed that both species stability and species asynchrony decreased with stand age (Fig. 1, estimate [±SE] = −0.258 [0.015], t = −17.655, P < 0.001 for species stability and estimate [±SE] = −0.022 [0.004], t = −5.822, P < 0.001 for species asynchrony). Besides spatial asynchrony, stand age was the major driver for stability at multiple scales (Supplementary Fig. 3A and Supplementary Table 1). Similar results were found in our sensitivity analysis which considered detrended stability (Supplementary Fig. 4), different ecoregions (Supplementary Fig. 5), other confounding variables (Supplementary Fig. 6A and Supplementary Fig. 7; observational frequency, survey interval, initial survey year, and final survey year), stand structure (Supplementary Fig. 8), and biomass loss due to mortality (Supplementary Fig. 8). Decreasing mean productivity and increasing standard deviation of productivity with stand age jointly contributed to successional declines in temporal stability (Supplementary Fig. 9 and Supplementary Fig. 10).

Stand age reduce diversity at multiple scales
Functional diversity at both the metacommunity scale and the local community scale decreased with stand age, but functional dissimilarity among local communities increased with stand age (Fig. 3, estimate [±SE] = −0.025 [0.007], t = −3.423, P < 0.001 for local functional diversity, estimate [±SE] = 0.039 [0.015], t = 2.613, P = 0.009 for functional dissimilarity among local communities, and estimate [±SE] = −0.020 [0.009], t = −2.210, P = 0.027 for metacommunity functional diversity). After considering confounding factors (observational frequency, survey interval, initial survey year, and final survey year), the trends of functional diversity with stand age at multiple spatial scales remained unchanged (Supplementary Figs. 3B, Supplementary Fig. 6B, and Supplementary Table S2). Similar results were found using the Shannon diversity index, but there was a non-significant relationship between metacommunity diversity and stand age (Fig. 3, estimate [±SE] = −0.018 [0.005], t = −3.364, P < 0.001 for local Shannon diversity, estimate [±SE] = 0.063 [0.002], t = 3.656, P < 0.001 for composition dissimilarity among local communities, and estimate [±SE] = −0.008 [0.008], t = −1.042, P = 0.297 for metacommunity Shannon diversity).

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This paper investigates how the temporal stability of forest productivity at multiple spatial scales changes with stand age and how this change is related to diversity during succession. Using a space-for-time substitution method, the authors found that the temporal stability of forest productivity decreases with stand age at both local and metacommunity scales. The findings of this study, such as older forests being less stable and the dominance of conservative species reducing species stability, differ from classic ecological theories. If accurate, these results would challenge established succession theories and our understanding of forest development in the United States. However, I recommend that the authors provide more detailed evidence supporting the reliability of their data analysis, to ensure the robustness and validity of their results and conclusions.
<General concerns>
Space-for-time substitutions, while useful, must be carefully employed. This approach has often been misused, leading to inaccurate conclusions about ecological patterns and processes (Walker et al. 2010; Damgaard 2019). Unfortunately, this paper appears to fall into this category, as it examines plots across the United States with varying ecoregions, climates, vegetation types, and soil conditions. It is challenging to believe that all these plots with different stand ages are comparable, and would follow the same successional trajectory. There are many confounding factors beyond stand age that could influence changes in diversity and stability. These factors should be considered and controlled during the analysis. For example, the authors could compare the temporal stability of plots with the same vegetation form, ecoregion, and soil type to ensure more accurate comparison. Additionally, it would be beneficial to assess whether climate and soil variables play more significant roles in driving stability changes than stand ages. The authors should perform more sensitivity analyses to validate and explain why their space-for-time substitution is valid. Without careful consideration of these factors, it is difficult to have confidence in the study’s conclusions.
The conceptual figure (Fig. 1) aligns better with the common understanding of forest succession, where community stability increases from young to mature forests and may decrease in old forests due to natural tree mortality. It is harder to believe that community stability consistently and linearly decreases over succession than to consider that the space-for-time substitution might be invalid. Given that many plots have a stand age of less than 50 years and are still in the early stages of succession, it is crucial to clarify the model selection process.
